extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator — literate English gentlemen and ladies (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on social behaviour, fashion, honour, conversation, and fan etiquette for men and women in early 18th‑century Britain, blending moral argument, practical instruction, and examples. Includes rules of taste (head-dress), points of honour, conversational decorum, and a detailed 'fan' etiquette/exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive head-dress / respect natural beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not add supernumerary ornaments to the head; Nature has designed the head as the 'Master-piece' and 'Cupola' of the human figure, and loading it with large artificial structures destroys the symmetry and calls off the eye from real beauties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and examples: extreme 'Fontanges' (tall cone/spire headdresses) exaggeratedly enlarged women's stature; such ornaments distract from face, hair, and natural features. Prevention: recommend addressing extravagance when fashion is against it; appeal to modesty and the futility of adding to what Nature has perfected.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to attack a fashion's extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective time to legislate or preach against the excesses of fashion is when the fashion itself is waning or against the extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical guidance: act as a preventive measure — recommend presenting arguments 'by way of Prevention' to readers (here, female readers) so that fashions do not resume after temporary suppression (example: Thomas Conecte's temporary triumph and the subsequent reappearance of Fontanges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of honour: courage for men, chastity for women
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief point of honour is courage in men and chastity in women; these are the qualifications each sex values most because they render them amiable to the opposite sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual nuance: alternative virtues (wisdom, virtue, wit, good-nature) might be chosen absent opposite-sex opinion. In chivalric/romantic literature these two qualities are treated as the central tests of worth (examples given from Books of Chivalry and Spanish custom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving the lie is the gravest affront between men
rubrics_metrics.description: The great violation of the point of honour from man to man is 'giving the lie' — calling a man a liar is an affront that commonly demands blood to expiate because lying implies cowardice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and cultural practice: because a lie implies lack of courage, accusing someone of lying touches the most sensitive part of honour. Historical aside: Herodotus' account of Persian instruction in truth-telling supports the value placed on speaking truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose false honour and duelling; use shame as deterrent
rubrics_metrics.description: The false notion of honour (that makes fighting and duelling glorious) should be combatted; public shame (for example, making those who fought duels stand in the pillory) would be an effective deterrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy recommendation: when honour's dictates contradict religion and equity they are 'the greatest Depravations' and should be 'exploded by all Governments.' Use of infamy/shame is advocated because death alone does not deter those who glorify risking life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate good humour and the disposition to be pleased
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a duty to cultivate a disposition to be pleased and place oneself in a constant aptitude for the satisfactions of being; mutual good humour is a social 'dress' one ought to wear in company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical signs and anti-patterns: avoid affecting delicacy (valetudinarians) who constantly complain of ailments, and avoid indolence (which reduces life to mere vegetative existence). Good humour seasons all encounters: be ready to set things in the best light, avoid shocking others, and be a welcome presence even if one contributes nothing wittily memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational decorum: present things in their excellence; avoid shocking topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation should aim to entertain by representing things in their best light; one should avoid presenting deformities or shocking matters and instead strive for delicate entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-ordered company expects to hear nothing that shocks and to have things set before them in excellence. The metaphor: when the cook has nothing but the best to hand, the entertainment is delicate. Thus select topics and tone to please and avoid dwelling on unpleasantness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and plainness over hollow compliment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and plainness in conversation are preferable to an excess of compliment and dissimulation; words should correspond to the heart and not be mere 'cyphers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and practical consequences: hollow compliments may be justified as 'Words are like Money' if everyone understands the current value, but they are still worthless; dissimulation leads to perpetual suspicion and loss of reputation — once integrity is forfeited, neither truth nor falsehood will serve the deceived party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fans as social instruments: formalized fan 'exercise' and meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: The fan is treated as a social 'weapon' with an art and a vocabulary — ladies should be trained in a formal 'Exercise of the Fan' comprising commands: Handle, Unfurl, Discharge, Ground, Recover, Flutter — each motion has prescribed form and social meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional specifics and learning timeline: 'Handle your Fans' (basic posture) learned in a week; 'Unfurl' (flirts, vibrations, gradual openings) may require a month; 'Discharge' (a loud crack) is difficult but trainable; 'Ground' (quit the fan gracefully) can be learned in two days; 'Recover' is simple; 'Flutter' (the master-piece) takes about three months and is taught in certain seasons. Types of flutter (angry, modest, timorous, confused, merry, amorous) correspond to emotions; the teacher claims ability to read a woman's feeling by her fan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach men the art of gallanting a fan and make practical tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Men (young gentlemen) should be instructed in the art of gallanting a fan; simpler, inexpensive fans can be made for training to avoid expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: the author offers to teach gentlemen and has invented plain practice-fans and even a fan design that amplifies sound (so a young girl may match an older woman's 'discharge'). A 'Treatise — The Passions of the Fan' is proposed as further elaboration.
